## Part 1: Restaurant Health Inspections (25 points)

The first dataset contains restaurant health inspection scores from Montgomery County. Load the data from: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/montco_inspections.csv`

The dataset includes the name of the establishment, the number of points for critical and non-critical areas, the total points, maximum points possible, the compliance score, and the grade.

### Task 1: Read the data (2 points)

```{r}
inspectionscores <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/montco_inspections.csv")
```

### Task 2: Calculate the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum of compliance scores. Save the results in a new dataframe called `compliance_stats`. (6 points)

```{r}
compliance_stats <- inspectionscores |> 
  summarize(mean = mean(compliance_score), sd = sd(compliance_score), min = min(compliance_score), max = max(compliance_score))
compliance_stats
```

### Task 3: Create a histogram of the compliance scores with a vertical line showing the mean. Include a headline and label the x and y axes. (8 points)

```{r}
inspectionscores |>
ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = compliance_score), binwidth = 4) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(compliance_score)), color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Compliance scores for Montgomery County restaurants",
       x = "Compliance Score",
       y = "Number of occurrences",
       caption = "Source: Montgomery County health inspection data")
```

### Task 4: Write 2–3 sentences interpreting what the standard deviation and histogram tell us about the distribution of compliance scores. What would be newsworthy about this distribution? What's the story here? (9 points)

#Keeping in mind the 68-95-99.7 rule for normal distributions, the standard deviation of this score tells us that 95% of restaurants score at least an 84.66 (2 standard distributions below the mean) and 99.7% of restaurants score at least a 78.84 (three standard distributions below the mean) on the compliance test, meaning nearly all restaurants in Montgomery County will have a score that is theoretically "acceptable" to patrons. This is backed up by the histogram, which shows an overwhelming amount of restaurants scored between 97 and 100 (at least, judging from the binwidth of 4 that I set). The fact that one standard deviation above the mean will go over 100, the maximum value for this test, also indicates that a lot of restaurants score perfectly or near-perfectly, which would be newsworthy in an ideal world; however, there would also be a compelling story about the 0.15% of restaurants that scored below the 78.84, which would be strengthened by reporting on where they are located, what sort of food was served, etc., in an attempt to find a common thread for these statistical outliers.

## Part 2: Daily Transit Ridership — Z-Scores (30 points)

Your editor wants you to identify unusual days in WMATA's daily ridership data that might be worth investigating as story leads. The dataset contains daily bus and rail totals, along with the day of the week. Load the data from: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/wmata_daily.csv`

### Task 5: Load the WMATA ridership data. (2 points)

```{r}
wmata_ridedata <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/wmata_daily.csv")
```

### Task 6: Using `mutate()`, add a column called `rail_zscore` that is the z-score for rail ridership, calculated using the overall mean and standard deviation of all days. Save the result as `wmata_zscores`. (7 points)

```{r}
wmata_zscores <- wmata_ridedata |>
  mutate(rail_zscore = ((rail - mean(rail)) / sd(rail))
           )
```

### Task 7: Rail ridership varies a lot by day of the week. Using `group_by()` and `mutate()`, add a column called `weekday_zscore` that calculates each day's rail z-score relative to other days with the same `weekday` (for example, a Sunday compared to other Sundays). Remember to `ungroup()` and save the result back to `wmata_zscores`. (8 points)

```{r}

wmata_zscores <- wmata_zscores %>%
  group_by(weekday) %>%
  mutate(
    daily_mean = mean(rail),
    daily_sd = sd(rail),
    weekday_zscore = (rail - daily_mean) / daily_sd
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

### Task 8: Filter for days where the absolute value of `rail_zscore` is greater than 2, and separately for days where the absolute value of `weekday_zscore` is greater than 2. Arrange each so the most extreme days appear first. How many unusual days does each method find? (5 points)

```{r}
wmata_zscores |>
filter(abs(rail_zscore) > 2) |> arrange(desc(abs(rail_zscore)))
wmata_zscores |>
filter(abs(weekday_zscore) > 2) |> arrange(desc(abs(weekday_zscore)))
```

#The first method found 10 unusual days in terms of z-scores, while the second method found 38 unusual days in terms of z-scores.

### Task 9: Write 2–3 sentences: How do the two lists of unusual days differ, and what story leads does each suggest? (8 points)

#The first list includes primarily holidays and days in January, and almost all of those z-scores are negative, which doesn't say much, as it's a little bit "no duh" that travel decreases on holidays where people stay in and immediately following the Christmas/New Year rush. The second list, meanwhile, has several other days that do not include holidays, while it also has some Tuesdays and Fridays, which were absent as days of the week on the first list. March 29, 2025 is a major statistical outlier, as is March 30 -- it commands a story on what happened on that weekend (there's nothing off the top of my head that would explain that, potentially a No Kings?), as do the other days that are two standard deviations above the average, as it is more unusual for there to be outliers with high levels of traffic.

## Part 3: Maryland Car Theft Rates (25 points)

Your editor has assigned you a story about car thefts in Maryland and wants you to find out which counties have the highest rates and which saw the biggest changes. The dataset contains car theft counts for Maryland counties in 2023 and 2024 along with population figures. Load the data from: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/md_car_thefts.csv`

### Task 10: Load the car thefts data. (2 points)

```{r}
md_car_thefts <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/md_car_thefts.csv")
```

### Task 11: Using `mutate()`, add two columns: `theft_rate`, the 2024 car theft rate per 10,000 residents, and `pct_change`, the percent change in thefts from 2023 to 2024. Save the result back to `md_car_thefts`. (10 points)

```{r}
md_car_thefts <- md_car_thefts |> mutate(
  theft_rate = (thefts_2024 / population * 10000),
  pct_change = ((thefts_2024 - thefts_2023) / thefts_2023 * 100)
)
```


### Task 12: Show the five counties with the highest 2024 theft rate, the five with the largest percent increase, and the five with the largest percent decrease. (5 points)

```{r}
md_car_thefts |> arrange(desc(thefts_2024))
md_car_thefts |> arrange(desc(pct_change))
md_car_thefts |> arrange((pct_change))
```

### Task 13: Write 2–3 sentences describing what these calculations reveal about car thefts in Maryland. What is the lede of a story based on your findings? (8 points)

#This data shows that overall, and particularly within the worst offending counties in terms of car thefts in Maryland, car thefts decreased from 2023 to 2024. In every county with at least 2,000 car thefts in 2023, the number of cars stolen dropped by at least 5% — and as much as 38% in Baltimore City, a remarkable achievement.

## Part 4: Data Analysis Scenario (20 points)

A county parks department releases data showing that its 12 community swimming pools average 187 visitors per day during the summer season, with a standard deviation of 42 visitors across the pools' average daily attendance. Your editor suspects that a handful of pools are dramatically underperforming and wants a story. You also learn that the department's figures are based on a random sample of 60 days per pool rather than a complete count.

Write 4–5 sentences for each of the following questions:

### Question A: How would you use descriptive statistics and z-scores to identify which pools are genuinely underperforming, and why is that more useful than simply ranking pools by raw attendance? (10 points)

#Ranking pools by raw attendance will lead to an overexaggeration of the significance of some data in one direction or the other based on the number of people who attend that pool — a pool that had averaged 600 visitors per day is going to have a very different reaction to having 10 fewer visitors on average per day. Z-scores will help to normalize the comparisons across pools dealing with different average crowd sizes, allowing for there to be better comparisons. The standard deviation will be useful in showing how consistent one pool's crowd is, and by extension, how variable their problems are. Mean and median numbers will also help to provide a good context for what a "normal" day at one pool would have looked like during that year. These descriptive statistics and z-scores are vital to actually having a good story.  

### Question B: The department collected its attendance figures using a random sample of 60 days per pool rather than tracking every day. What questions would you ask about the sample before relying on these figures for a story? What concerns would you raise in your story? (10 points)

#The very first question that I have regarding this sample is whether the sample was truly random, as I wouldn't necessarily trust that they'd pick a true random. I'd also have to confirm whether they used the same days for each pool, as that would be necessary to confirm the validity of the test. I would also be concerned about whether this random sample was truly representative in terms of the weather shown on the days and the days of the week sampled, as a sample that weighted factors that would impact whether or not people would choose to go to the pool too imprecisely would have low external validity. I'd be concerned that aside from not necessarily being representative of the summer's true conditions, they would too heavily weight this one summer, which may be abnormal compared to other summers that the state has experienced.
